meta.title: Who really said "Choose a job you love, and you will never have to work a day in your life"? | Quotle.info
meta.description: No — Confucius never said it. The earliest known version is a 1982 Princeton Alumni Weekly citation; it was first credited to Confucius in 1985.
meta.ogTitle: Who really said 'Choose a job you love, and you will never have to work a day in your life'?
meta.ogDescription: No — Confucius never said it. Earliest known version: a 1982 Princeton Alumni Weekly citation. First pinned on Confucius in 1985.

answer.label: Not Confucius — an anonymous modern American saying
answer.authorDates: Earliest documented 1982 · falsely credited to Confucius from 1985
answer.sourceLine: There is no evidence Confucius wrote or said this, and it appears in none of his works. The earliest documented version — “Find something you love to do and you’ll never have to work a day in your life” — was recorded in the Princeton Alumni Weekly in 1982, and even that speaker credited an unnamed “old-timer.” It was first attached to Confucius only in 1985.

source.heading: Where the saying actually comes from
source.excerpt: Find something you love to do and you’ll never have to work a day in your life.
trail: The Quote Investigator investigation traces the earliest strong match to the Princeton Alumni Weekly of 6 October 1982, where Prof. Arthur Szathmary used it and credited an unidentified source.
The first time the saying was pinned on Confucius, per QI, was an epigraph in the trade journal Computerworld on 3 June 1985 — the words are described there as “the first linkage to the luminary.”
Wikiquote files the line under “Misattributed,” noting it has been credited to Confucius “since at least 1985” and that “correct origins are dubious.”
source.excerptNote: The oldest known form, quoted by Princeton philosophy professor Arthur Szathmary in 1982, who himself credited an unnamed “old-timer.” The now-standard “Choose a job you love…” wording and the Confucius label came later.
source.rightsNote: Because the exact wording has no identified author — it surfaces anonymously in the early 1980s and its true originator is unknown — no copyright status can be responsibly asserted. It is certainly not an ancient public-domain text of Confucius; the modern English phrasing is a 20th-century saying of untraced authorship.

author.name: Confucius
author.heading: About Confucius
author.metaLine: 551–479 BC · Chinese philosopher & teacher (the misattributed figure)
author.bio: Confucius (Kongzi) was a Chinese teacher and philosopher of the Spring and Autumn period whose sayings, compiled by disciples in the Analects, shaped East Asian ethics for millennia. His genuine teachings emphasize duty, ritual propriety, and social harmony — not a modern career-happiness slogan. His fame makes him one of the internet’s top magnets for feel-good lines he never uttered, and this is one of them.

misattribution.heading: The Confucius label is a modern invention
misattribution.intro: This is a textbook “wisdom-sounding line pinned on a famous sage” case. The thought is a modern American career aphorism; Confucius’s name was attached decades after his death by nearly 2,500 years.

items.why: The line appears nowhere in the Analects or any Confucian text. Quote Investigator found no evidence for it and calls the linkage to Confucius “spurious”; the notion of freely choosing a job you love is also anachronistic for his era.
Per QI, the first Confucius attribution was a 1985 Computerworld epigraph by Glenn Rifkin; motivational author Harvey Mackay later helped popularize the saying, though he did not originate it.

misattribution.truthLine: The real record: an anonymous modern proverb, earliest seen in the Princeton Alumni Weekly (1982) — credited by its own speaker to an unnamed “old-timer,” not to Confucius.
